title: What the principles are (and are not)
statement: Proportionality, parsimony, totality, parity and the prohibitions on double punishment and crushing sentences are guiding or limiting principles of broad application. They are not a blueprint, do not dictate a path of reasoning, and are taken together with gravity, purposes, the circumstances of offence and offender, and policy considerations.

refs.q: However, as is clear from the quote above, the principles are not a blueprint for determining sentence. They do not dictate a path of reasoning to be followed. They are either guiding or limiting principles of broad application, but they do not add up to a closed system for sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles

title: Proportionality
statement: The sentence should be proportionate to the gravity of the offence in light of the circumstances, including the maximum penalty, the harm, the method and the offender's culpability; it constrains both leniency and severity. The maximum defines the limit for the worst class of offending but is a guidepost. A longer term cannot be imposed merely to cure a condition (including addiction), to protect the community or for preventative detention. It applies to the total effective sentence, parity, mitigation, aggregation, cumulation and the non-parole period. There is no single proportionate sentence and sentencing is not a stepped process that first fixes a proportionate term. Legislation qualifies the principle to some degree (serious offenders under s 6D; indefinite sentences), but proportionality remains a fundamental consideration: departure is sparing and must be reasoned (see principle.proportionality_detail).

refs.q: The principle of proportionality defines the upper and lower limits of punishment. It constrains both excessively lenient and overly severe responses to crime.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: It is a well-established principle that says that the sentence imposed should be proportionate to the gravity of the offence considered in the light of the circumstances, including the maximum statutory penalty for the offence, the degree of harm, the method of committing the offence, and the offender’s culpability.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: The maximum penalty, however, is only a guidepost for fixing an appropriate sentence, and a lengthy term cannot be imposed merely to cure an offender’s condition (including drug addiction), to protect the community or to further preventative detention (even in cases of terrorism).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: The proportionality principle applies to all aspects of sentencing, including the total effective sentence, parity, mitigation, aggregation, cumulation, and the fixing of a non-parole period or suspended sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: There is no single proportionate sentence and an attempt to fix one before fixing the sentence to be imposed will only multiply the possibilities of error.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: But the principle is qualified to some degree by legislation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: But this does not oblige a judge to disregard the principle of proportionality. It remains a fundamental consideration and the power to depart from it should be exercised sparingly, with adequate reasons given for any decision to do so.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

title: Parsimony and the hierarchy of sanctions (s 5(3)–(7))
statement: The sentence must be no more severe than necessary to achieve the purposes (type and length). In general, imprisonment cannot be imposed unless the purposes cannot be achieved by any other sentence, nor where a drug treatment order or CCO will serve; a drug treatment order not where a CCO suffices; a CCO not where a fine will do; a fine not where a dismissal, discharge or adjournment is sufficient. No single less severe sentence is mandated, and reasons for rejecting a non-custodial term are not required.

refs.q: It is a common law rule that requires the sentence be no more severe than is necessary to achieve the sentencing purposes. Although often concerned with the type of sanction to be imposed, parsimony also applies to the length of the sanction.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.2 – Parsimony

refs.q: A sentence of imprisonment also may not be imposed where a drug treatment order or conditional Community Corrections Order (‘CCO’) will serve the sentencing purposes. Further, a drug treatment order cannot be imposed where a CCO will suffice, a CCO must not be imposed where a fine will do, and a fine cannot be imposed if a dismissal, discharge or adjournment is sufficient.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.2 – Parsimony

refs.q: The court is not required to give reasons for rejecting a non-custodial term,
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.2 – Parsimony

refs.q: In general, it means only that a sentence of imprisonment cannot be imposed unless the purposes for which the sentence is imposed cannot be achieved by any other sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.2 – Parsimony

title: Totality
statement: For multiple offences the aggregate must be a just and appropriate measure of the total criminality. Preferred approach: appropriate individual terms, then wholly or partly concurrent orders — not cumulation of artificially reduced sentences. Steps: an appropriate term for each charge (highest as base — but see Barbat, fn 450); decide cumulation; then stand back and consider the appropriate total effective sentence, moderating cumulation if needed. The secondary "moderate and cumulate" approach is available where the preferred approach is not possible. Totality applies to offences that may overlap or be cumulated on an existing custodial sentence, to sentences imposed at the same time and to offences committed on different occasions and in different States (authority conflicts on whether interstate offending must be close in time and similar in kind, so care is needed), and to the head sentence and the non-parole period.
note: fn 450 (“But see Barbat”) is attached to the step designating the highest term as the base sentence; the Manual records the contrary authority without resolving it.

refs.q: The totality principle requires a court in sentencing an offender for multiple offences to ensure that the aggregate term it imposes is ‘a just and appropriate measure of the total criminality involved’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: To fashion an appropriate total effective head term that satisfies the requirements of totality, it is preferable to impose appropriate individual terms, which satisfy all the sentencing objectives, and then make them wholly or partially concurrent, ‘rather than by an order or orders for the cumulation of unnecessarily reduced individual sentences’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: • Determine an appropriate term for each charge, taking the applicable sentencing considerations into account, and designate the highest term as the base sentence. • Determine the extent to which there should be cumulation regarding each count. • Then ‘stand back’ and consider, in light of the totality principle, what is an appropriate total effective sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: The totality principle also applies to fixing of the head sentence and the non-parole period,
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: The totality principle applies when sentencing for offences that may overlap or be cumulated upon an existing custodial sentence. It applies not only to multiple sentences imposed at the same time, but to sentences imposed for offences committed on different occasions and in different States.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: There is conflicting authority on whether such interstate offending must be close in time and of a similar kind, so sentencing in such circumstances requires care.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: But see Barbat v The Queen [2014] VSCA 202, [49], [51], [72] (‘Barbat’).

title: Totality, serious offenders (ss 6D, 6E) and parole offending (ss 5(2AA), 16(3B))
statement: Section 6D affects totality much as it affects proportionality: the court must be satisfied the offender will remain a danger beyond the period totality would permit. Totality must not be applied as if s 6E (presumptive cumulation for serious offenders) did not exist. For offending on parole: the court must not speculate on future executive action (s 5(2AA)), but where parole has been cancelled it considers the whole of the prior sentence with the new one so that the combination is not disproportionate to the aggregated criminality; absent exceptional circumstances the new sentence is cumulative (s 16(3B)) and totality cannot be applied inconsistently with that. Where parole has not been cancelled at the time of sentencing, no s 16(3B) order (cumulation or concurrency) may be made without breaching s 5(2AA) (see flag.parole_not_cancelled_at_sentence: s 77(7A) deems cancellation at sentence).

refs.q: ‘[i]t would be wrong to ‘direct otherwise’ simply in order to achieve what totality might have required in the absence of s 6E’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

refs.q: The sentencing court must be satisfied that the combined effect of the two is not ‘disproportionate to the aggregated criminality involved in the breach offending and the prior offending’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: A court must give effect to this intention and must not apply the principle of totality to the extent that it is inconsistent.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: Note that unlike cases where parole has been cancelled prior to sentencing for the offences committed on parole, where parole has not been cancelled at the time of sentencing, the court may not make an order pursuant to s 16(3B) for cumulation or concurrency without breaching s 5(2AA).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has held that this section has substantially the same impact on totality as it does on proportionality because the sentencing court will have to be satisfied that the offender ‘will remain a danger to the community beyond the period that totality would permit’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

title: Double punishment
statement: A person must not be punished twice for the same criminal conduct: where offences share elements, the common elements must not be punished twice. Approach it as common sense, not semantics. If one offence is wholly subsumed in another, do not sentence for the subsumed offence (even concurrently). A single act causing separate harms (especially to different people) may be punished separately. The test is whether one sentence includes punishment also included in the other. Aggregate sentences rarely raise the issue.

refs.q: The rule states that a person must not be punished twice for the same criminal conduct. Specifically, to the extent two offences contain common elements, it is wrong to punish an offender ‘twice for commission of the elements that are common’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: The enquiry must be approached as a matter of common sense, not as a matter of semantics. If the elements of one offence are wholly subsumed within another, then an offender should not be sentenced for the subsumed offence, not even if the sentence is made entirely concurrent with the primary sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: But where a single act reflects separate harms, particularly separate harms against different people, each may be punished separately, even when linked by time and place.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: The test is whether in the process of arriving at sentences for overlapping offending, a court includes in one sentence an element of punishment that is also included in the other.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.2 – Harm to/Endangering the person

refs.q: Cumulating a sentence for the summary offence of driving with more than the prescribed concentration of alcohol in the blood on a sentence for culpable driving also doubly punishes an offender as the level of alcohol in the blood is an element of both offences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.4 – Driving offences

title: Avoiding a crushing sentence
statement: A court should not impose a crushing sentence (one destroying any reasonable expectation of a useful life after release) unless there are special circumstances — eg crimes arousing deep public revulsion, a persistent unrepentant offender, multiple grave crimes, or community protection. It is an expression of the rehabilitation principle; a richly deserved sentence is not disturbed because the offender may feel crushed; age is relevant but cannot support an inappropriate sentence. The Manual also says there is no sentencing principle that requires a crushing sentence to be avoided, describing it as a particular expression of the rehabilitation principle (principle.crushing_detail); the two statements are recorded in flag.crushing_sentence_principle ((app policy) a possibly crushing total is a caution, never an error).

refs.q: A court should not impose a ‘crushing sentence’ unless there are special circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: A ‘crushing sentence’ is so long that it might provoke a feeling of helplessness in the offender (if and) when they’re released or destroy any reasonable expectation they have for a useful life after release.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: ‘A richly deserved sentence…is not to be disturbed because the offender may feel crushed by it’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: ‘Special circumstances’ may include crimes that arouse deep public revulsion or disquiet, crimes committed by a persistent and unrepentant offender, or by an offender who has committed multiple crimes of considerable gravity.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: But there is no sentencing principle that requires a crushing sentence to be avoided. It is a particular expression of the principle that wherever possible a sentence should be imposed to promote the rehabilitation of the offender and there will be occasions when the offending is so grave that little weight can be given in the sentencing calculus to promoting the offender’s rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

title: Parity between co-offenders
statement: Like cases should be treated alike: any significant difference between co-offenders' sentences should be capable of a rational explanation (an evaluation by impression). Relevant differences include age, background, criminal history, health, character and role (instigator, recruiter or principal vs aider and abettor or subordinate); also significant assistance to police and prosecution (possibly even where the non-cooperating offender was subordinate), an early plea (not a “marked” disparity — but see Sikoulabout, fn 589), adult vs juvenile (parity has only a limited application), armed vs unarmed, differences in criminal history, moral culpability and gain, dependence on or domination by the other in a personal or familial relationship, and personal factors (rehabilitation, specific deterrence, impact of custody, mercy). Compare all components including non-parole periods. Where parity requires modification, err on the side of leniency. Using a co-offender's sentence as a starting point and adjusting is an inappropriate two-step process.

refs.q: The concept is simply that when two or more co-offenders are sentenced, any significant difference in the sentences imposed upon them should be capable of a rational explanation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Their ages, backgrounds, criminal history, health, characters, and roles played in the offending are all relevant and may justify disparate sentences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: However, the willingness of one offender to plead guilty earlier than another co-offender, does not justify a ‘marked’ disparity in sentences between the two;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Comparison of the head sentence alone is not an adequate measure of parity. All components of the sentence (including any non-parole period) must be considered, and if totality requires different sentences between the co-offenders, then parity is not breached.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Where parity does require modification of the sentence to be imposed, it is appropriate to err on the side of leniency and eliminate or diminish the appearance of injustice by reducing the more severe penalty, even where it is otherwise appropriate and within the permissible range of sentencing options.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Although there is no dictated sentencing sequence, using the sentence of a co-offender as a starting point and then reducing or increasing the sentence being imposed based on other factors is an inappropriate two-step process.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: • between offenders who instigate the offending, recruit their co-offender, are a principal, or have a more preeminent role in the offending, and those who are an aider and abettor, subordinate, or recruit;

refs.q: • if one offender provides significant assistance to the police and prosecution. Depending on the circumstances this may be so even if the non-cooperating offender was a subordinate in the criminal enterprise;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: • between adult and juvenile co-offenders. Parity has only a limited application to these offenders because they are sentenced under different systems where different principles apply.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: • if an offender was armed, whether the weapon is loaded or not, and their co-offender was not;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: • due to differences in the co-offender’s criminal histories, moral culpability, and any gain (financial or otherwise) from the offending;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: • for co-offenders in personal or familial relationships, where one is dependent upon, dominated, or led by the other;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: • by matters that are personal to the offender such as their prospects for rehabilitation, the importance of deterring them in future, the impact of incarceration on them, or the imposition of a lenient sentence as an exercise of mercy (usually because one offender is gravely ill);

title: Interaction between totality, parity and crushing sentences
statement: Different sentences required by totality do not breach parity; disparity explained by differences in criminal histories and/or an application of totality gives no justifiable grievance; a sentence may offend totality without being crushing (but some authority treats avoiding a crushing sentence as part of the totality analysis: flag.crushing_within_totality).

refs.q: ‘[W]here the totality principle is relevant in the sentencing process and the application of that principle requires different sentences for each offender, no breach of the parity principle occurs’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.4 – Interaction with the other principles

refs.q: A crushing sentence is not one that inherently offends the principle of totality.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.4 – Interaction with the other principles

refs.q: Disparity in sentences between co-offenders will not give rise to a justifiable sense of grievance where it can be explained by differences in their criminal histories ‘and/or an application of the totality principle’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.4 – Interaction with the other principles

title: The purposes of sentencing (s 5(1))
statement: Just punishment; deterrence of the offender and others; rehabilitation; denunciation; protection of the community. They overlap, can point in different directions, and which (if any) is paramount is a discretionary matter in all the circumstances.

refs.q: • punish the offender in a manner which is just in all the circumstances; • deter the offender and others from committing the same or a similar offence; • facilitate an offender’s rehabilitation; • denounce the offending conduct; and • protect the community.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: More than one purpose may be (and often is) furthered by a given sentence, and determining which purpose, if any, is paramount depends on all circumstances and is a discretionary matter for the sentencing court.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: As the High Court put it in Veen v The Queen (No 2), ‘[t]hey are guideposts to the appropriate sentence, but sometimes they point in different directions’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: The Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) (‘the Act’) states that the purposes of sentencing are to:

title: Just punishment and denunciation
statement: Just punishment reflects the moral sense of the community; it synthesises the offender's circumstances, the gravity of the crime and current sentencing practices (not mechanically). It is significant for homicide (especially domestic), causing serious injury (especially family violence), culpable or dangerous driving, armed robbery, aggravated burglary and sex offences (especially against children or vulnerable people). Denunciation communicates society's condemnation of the conduct (not the person). The victim's rehabilitation is relevant. Denunciation and retribution have less relevance for a mentally disabled offender unable to appreciate condemnation; a deliberate affront by an able offender cannot expect leniency; for grave crimes rehabilitation of a youth gives way.

refs.q: Imposing a just sentence requires a court to synthesise different factors, including the offender’s circumstances (but not their expectations), the circumstances and gravity of the crime, and current sentencing practices.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: Just punishment is a significant consideration in cases of: • homicide, particularly of a domestic partner or family member; • causing serious injury, again with special relevance in situations involving domestic or family violence; • culpable or dangerous driving; • armed robbery; • aggravated burglary; and • sex offences, especially against children or vulnerable people.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: It requires a sentence to communicate – through its type or duration – society’s condemnation and disapproval of the conduct;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: Moreover, the rehabilitation of the victim is a relevant factor to be considered.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: the retributive effect and denunciatory aspect of a sentence have less relevance to a mentally disabled offender who is incapable of appreciating the societal condemnation of the sentence,
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: Although it is the offender’s conduct that is denounced, and not the offender personally, there may be circumstances of the offender that are relevant both to denunciation and just punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: These purposes flow from the community’s expectation that certain offences deserve severe punishment, and the assumption that if this expectation is denied there is a danger respect for the law will be diminished and the community will take punishment into its own hands.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: This ‘social rehabilitation’ has not been given the attention it deserves and can be facilitated by the courts.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

title: Deterrence: points common to general and specific deterrence
statement: Deterrence is tempered by proportionality; it applies to the head sentence and the non-parole period (an unduly low non-parole period may destroy its effect); it may be achieved by non-custodial sentences. Mental illness or impairment may moderate or eliminate it (not automatically; moderation preferred), depending on symptoms and capacity; a condition arising from the reaction to discovery of the crime does not reduce it. Ideological or martyrdom motivation may make deterrence less relevant.
note: The suspended sentences 4.2 mentions are not available for offences committed after the dates in suspended.abolished (flag.suspended_on_date).

refs.q: Firstly, general and specific deterrence are tempered by the proportionality principle; a sentence cannot be so stern that it is disproportionate to the gravity of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: Thirdly, deterrence applies to both the head sentence and the non-parole period. But if a custodial sentence is warranted, fixing an unduly low non-parole period may destroy its deterrent effect.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: an offender’s mental illness or impairment may moderate or eliminate the importance of general and specific deterrence, but this is not automatic and sensible moderation is preferred over elimination.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: A reduction is not required, however, where the condition has arisen as a result of the crime’s discovery and the offender’s reaction to the possibility of a long prison term.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: Secondly, deterrence is most frequently discussed in terms of an immediate custodial sentence, but it may also be achieved by imposing a non-custodial sentence, including a wholly suspended sentence or a fine.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: Whether general or specific deterrence is moderated or eliminated depends on the nature and severity of the offender’s symptoms and the effect of the condition on their mental capacity at the time of offending or sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: Although a fine that is beyond the means of the offender to pay has no deterrent effect.
It is useful to bear in mind the difference between denunciation and deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: Denunciation is a symbolic community condemnation of the offender’s wrong, but deterrence is concerned with punishing the offender as a means of deterring others from committing a similar offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: There are two types of deterrence, as recognised by the Act, general and specific.

title: General deterrence
statement: General deterrence plays a role in almost every case but must not overwhelm the other purposes to produce a disproportionately harsh sentence, and must not target an ethnic community. Particularly important for homicide (domestic), indictable driving, child sexual offending, family violence, armed robbery, aggravated burglary, white collar crime, drug trafficking, prevalent offences, OHS offences, people smuggling and terrorism; and where public safety is at risk (street violence, drug/alcohol-fuelled or unprovoked violence, vulnerable victims, police, emergency workers, good Samaritans) or a court order (bail, parole, intervention order) is breached — there it “takes priority”. In some circumstances it may be moderated for an elderly offender (mercy may reduce its weight where death in prison is possible), but it remains important irrespective of advancing age. It has minimal relevance for a child, continues to have (moderated) relevance for an adult sentenced for offending committed as a child, is usually far less important than rehabilitation for youthful offenders except as seriousness rises, and may be given reduced weight for investigative or prosecutorial delay (not victim reluctance). Whether it applies to charges that could have been dealt with in the Children’s Court is unclear (flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges).

refs.q: General deterrence plays a role in almost every case.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: So, a court must be careful to ensure that general deterrence is not permitted to cause injustice, by so overwhelming the other sentencing purposes that an individual sentence becomes disproportionately harsh when assessed against the degree of criminality of an offender’s conduct.

refs.q: • homicide, especially in a domestic context; • indictable driving; • sexual offending against children; • family or domestic violence; • armed robbery; • aggravated burglary; • ‘white collar’ crimes, such as fraud, tax evasion or money laundering; • drug offences, particularly trafficking; • prevalent offences; • OH&S offences; • people smuggling; and • terrorist offences or preparing for terrorist acts.

refs.q: Moreover, general deterrence takes priority in circumstances where public safety is put at risk, as in cases involving street violence, and where violent acts are fueled by drugs or alcohol, or are unprovoked; where vulnerable members of the community, law enforcement officers, emergency care workers, or good Samaritans are victimised; or, if the offending is committed in breach of a court order, such as bail, parole or an intervention order.

title: Specific deterrence
statement: Criminal history is probably the most significant consideration; generally, the greater the risk of reoffending, the more weight. Persistent recidivism may preclude a moderate sentence; good character or a low risk of reoffending reduces but does not exclude it; offending while subject to another court order (bail, parole, an intervention order) requires it to be emphasised; it may assume great significance where the offence is a significant escalation of prior offending; it is less significant where the offender is genuinely remorseful, but good rehabilitation prospects do not make it irrelevant; a plea alone does not establish remorse.

refs.q: An offender’s criminal history is probably the most significant consideration in determining the importance of specific deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: Generally, the greater the risk of re-offending, the more weight is given to specific deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: But specific deterrence is only reduced, not excluded, where an offender is of good character or unlikely to re-offend.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: Nor does the mere entry of a guilty plea establish remorse; proper evidence is required.

refs.q: Persistent recidivism may also preclude a moderate sentence because it demonstrates that previously lenient sanctions have not proved effective.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: Relatedly, a person’s willingness to offend while subject to another court order, such as bail, parole, or an intervention order requires specific deterrence to be emphasised.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: Specific deterrence may also assume great significance where the subject offence represents a significant escalation of prior offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: Specific deterrence will be less significant where an offender is genuinely remorseful for their actions as it demonstrates an increased likelihood of rehabilitation and appreciation for the wrongfulness of their conduct.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: Every sentence is meant, in part, to have the salutary effect of deterring the offender being sentenced from future criminal conduct.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: But, again, there is no formula for determining a sentence that will have that effect; it is derived from a consideration of the circumstances of the offender and the offending.

refs.q: Most relevantly it may indicate whether they tend to disobey the law, and so require greater punishment to deter them in future.

title: Rehabilitation
statement: Steps towards rehabilitation should be given due weight, but the court does not set a period of rehabilitation or impose a disproportionate sentence to facilitate it. Rehabilitation has two parts — remorse and reform — both must be demonstrated. Relevant: plea, conduct of the defence, motive, delay not attributable to the offender, criminal record, youth (usually far more important than general deterrence), addiction, mental impairment. In serious, grave or violent offending other purposes may predominate. It may justify a lower non-parole period, but it is wrong to assume the head sentence reflects punishment and the non-parole period rehabilitation. A youthful first offender should not, if it can be avoided, be given a custodial sentence; alternatives like a youth justice centre are preferred to adult prison. Where an offender has had every opportunity to rehabilitate and has not done so, other purposes may take precedence; rehabilitation between absconding and new offending may be given slight weight.

refs.q: However, the court’s task is not to set a period of rehabilitation. Nor may it protect an offender by imposing a disproportionate sentence to emphasise and facilitate their rehabilitation.

statement: CCOs, deferral and the dismissal/discharge/adjournment orders promote rehabilitation in the community; not recording a conviction for serious offending is limited to 'out of the ordinary' or 'exceptional' circumstances that facilitate the offender's rehabilitation.

title: Protection of the community
statement: Protection is usually by incapacitation but not only by imprisonment; prior convictions showing a continuing attitude of disobedience for the law, reluctance to undergo treatment or an incurable disorder fuelling offending may raise its importance (possibly to primary importance). It is limited by proportionality — no disproportionate sentence to extend protection. Legislative exceptions arguably elevate protection above proportionality: s 6D (serious offenders) is permissive — the court “may” impose a disproportionate term, is not required to, and need not disregard proportionality; before doing so it must be satisfied the offender will remain a danger beyond a proportionate term, with reasons — and indefinite sentences.

refs.q: But the community may be protected by other means and imprisonment is not the only way to give effect to this purpose.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: A sentence must be proportionate to the crime, and a disproportionate sentence may not be imposed to extend the period of protection of society from the risk of recidivism on the part of an offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: And before imposing a disproportionate term to further the community’s protection, the court must also be satisfied that the prisoner will remain a danger to the community beyond the period proportionality would indicate is an appropriate term and it must provide reasons for doing so.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: There are legislative exceptions that arguably elevate the protective purpose above the requirements of proportionality.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: Moreover, the language of the Act is important: a court ‘may’ impose a disproportionate term. There is no requirement that it do so, nor that it disregard proportionality (or any other) principle.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: A person’s prior convictions may indicate a continuing attitude of disobedience for the law such that community protection assumes greater, if not primary, importance.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: Protecting the community from the danger posed by an offender is done by incapacitating them, which usually means removing them from society through the imposition of a custodial term.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: The second legislative exception allows a court sentencing a serious offender for a serious offence to impose an indefinite term if it is satisfied to a high degree of probability that the offender is a serious danger to the community because of their circumstances, the nature or gravity of the offending, or any special circumstances.

refs.q: An offender’s circumstances are often most relevant in determining the need for community protection.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: However, community protection is also largely limited by the proportionality principle.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

title: Why the principles are “fundamental” — and their limits
statement: The principles (proportionality, parsimony, totality, double punishment, crushing sentences, parity) are treated as fundamental because their application does not depend on the circumstances of the offence or offender and, subject to conditions and exceptions, they can make some claim to universal application. They are guiding or limiting principles, not a closed system: they are taken together with gravity, purposes, circumstances and policy in the synthesis.

refs.q: These principles are treated as fundamental because their application does not depend on the circumstances of the offence or the offender, and because, subject to the conditions and exceptions discussed below, they can make some claim to universal application in sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles

refs.q: They are either guiding or limiting principles of broad application, but they do not add up to a closed system for sentencing. They are considerations to be taken together with the gravity of the offence, the purposes of sentencing, the circumstances of the offence and offender, and relevant policy considerations, in the synthesis of a just and appropriate sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles

refs.q: This chapter examines these fundamental principles, and the prohibitions on double punishment and crushing sentences.

title: Proportionality: the maximum, its statutory qualifications, and no “stepped” proportionate term
statement: The maximum defines the absolute limit for the worst class of the offence but is only a guidepost; a lengthy term cannot be imposed merely to cure a condition (including addiction), to protect the community or for preventative detention. Legislation qualifies the principle: for a serious offender sentenced for a relevant offence, the Supreme or County Court must treat community protection as paramount and may impose a disproportionate sentence where necessary — but proportionality remains fundamental and departure must be sparing and reasoned; an indefinite sentence is confined to very exceptional cases. Proportionality applies to every aspect (total effective sentence, parity, mitigation, aggregation, cumulation, non-parole periods). Individual sentences must not be made artificially inadequate to accommodate cumulation; each count gets an appropriate and proportionate sentence. Sentencing is not a stepped process that first fixes a proportionate term: a range of proportionate sentences is usually open and there is no single one.

refs.q: The maximum penalty (if any) fixed by the legislature defines the absolute limit for the worst class of offending covered by the offence in question.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: The maximum penalty, however, is only a guidepost for fixing an appropriate sentence, and a lengthy term cannot be imposed merely to cure an offender’s condition (including drug addiction), to protect the community or to further preventative detention (even in cases of terrorism).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: Firstly, in sentencing a serious offender for a relevant offence, the Supreme or County Court must consider protection of the community to be the paramount sentencing purpose, and if the court considers it necessary to further that purpose it may impose a sentence longer than that which is proportionate to the gravity of the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: But this does not oblige a judge to disregard the principle of proportionality. It remains a fundamental consideration and the power to depart from it should be exercised sparingly, with adequate reasons given for any decision to do so.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: Secondly, a court may impose an indefinite sentence in respect of a serious offence where it is satisfied that the offender is a serious danger to the community. The exercise of this power is similarly confined to very exceptional cases where the exercise of the power is demonstrably necessary to protect society from physical harm.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: The proportionality principle applies to all aspects of sentencing, including the total effective sentence, parity, mitigation, aggregation, cumulation, and the fixing of a non-parole period or suspended sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: Artificially inadequate sentences should not be imposed to accommodate the mandates of cumulation. ‘Appropriate and proportionate sentences’ should be imposed on each individual count when there are multiple charges in the indictment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: Lastly, sentencing is not a stepped process that first requires a court to set a term proportionate to the crime. There is no justification for that approach, and it will produce inadequate sentences and injustice. Deciding what sentence is proportionate is a matter of discretion and in most cases a range of proportionate sentences is open. There is no single proportionate sentence and an attempt to fix one before fixing the sentence to be imposed will only multiply the possibilities of error.

title: Parsimony: what the hierarchy requires; reasons; supervision orders
statement: Before imposing imprisonment the judge must be satisfied that no other sentence is appropriate; the sentence must be no more severe than necessary (in type and length). The statutory hierarchy does not mean there is a single less severe sentence that must be imposed; in general it means imprisonment cannot be imposed unless the purposes cannot be achieved by any other sentence. The court need not give reasons for rejecting a non-custodial term or note parsimony expressly. Parsimony also applies to supervision orders under the Crimes (Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be Tried) Act.

refs.q: The principle of parsimony holds that a sentencing judge must satisfy themselves that no other sentence is appropriate before imposing a term of imprisonment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.2 – Parsimony

refs.q: This hierarchy does not mean there is a single less severe sentence that must be imposed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.2 – Parsimony

refs.q: In general, it means only that a sentence of imprisonment cannot be imposed unless the purposes for which the sentence is imposed cannot be achieved by any other sentence.

title: Totality: the preferred and secondary approaches, and when totality applies
statement: There must be appropriate relativity between the totality of the criminality and the total effective sentence. Individual sentences should not be made artificially inadequate to accommodate cumulation (they may be “modest”). The strongly preferred approach — appropriate individual terms, the highest as base, cumulation for each count, then “stand back” and moderate cumulation if the total infringes totality — should be departed from only for a special feature of the case; it is not mandatory, other consistent approaches are permissible and a different approach does not itself show error. Where it cannot be followed, the secondary “moderate and cumulate” approach (reduced individual terms, partly cumulated) may be used, e.g. where the offender has previously served substantial periods of imprisonment and conventional terms could produce a disproportionately long sentence, multiple serious offences, or where s 16(3B) precludes concurrency. The preferred approach exists so that each sentence reflects its offence, remaining sentences stay appropriate if one is set aside, and artificial disparity claims are avoided. A single court may achieve totality by concurrency (wholly or partly) or by disproportionately low terms. Totality applies when sentencing for offences that may overlap or be cumulated on an existing custodial sentence, to sentences imposed at the same time and to offences on different occasions and in different States (authority conflicts on whether interstate offending must be close in time and similar in kind: care), to head sentence and non-parole period, and where the current sentence derives from a parole breach. Usually the court considers what would have been just had all offences been sentenced together; where that is not apt (Sayer), totality applies distinctly and prior sentences and custody remain part of the offender’s circumstances (but see Mendoza-Cortez, fn 469).

refs.q: There must be appropriate relativity between the totality of all criminality and the totality of the effective length of the sentences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: But when sentencing for multiple offences, a court should not impose artificially inadequate sentences to accommodate cumulation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: The individual sentences may not be inadequate, but they may be ‘modest’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: It must be emphasised that this is a preferred approach, albeit a strongly preferred one that should be departed from only when a special feature of the case requires it.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: Nonetheless, it is not mandatory and there is more than one approach to the totality principle. So long as its approach is consistent and the sentence is in accordance with the relevant statutory regime, a court should be afforded great flexibility in sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: The fact that from time to time a court may approach the task differently than the preferred approach does not demonstrate error, especially if the total effective sentence and the non-parole period are within range.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: To comply with the totality principle, the basic sentencing steps that a court should follow are: • Determine an appropriate term for each charge, taking the applicable sentencing considerations into account, and designate the highest term as the base sentence. • Determine the extent to which there should be cumulation regarding each count. • Then ‘stand back’ and consider, in light of the totality principle, what is an appropriate total effective sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: If applying the first two steps produces a total effective sentence that infringes totality, the court should moderate the cumulation to ensure the total effective sentence complies.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: Generally, the imposition of less severe individual sentences may call for greater cumulation to reflect total criminality where more severe individual sentences may require greater concurrency.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: Where it is not possible to follow the preferred approach, a court may follow the secondary ‘moderate and cumulate’ approach of imposing reduced individual terms and then cumulating a portion of each to produce an appropriate total effective sentence. This may result in a head sentence that does not appropriately reflect the gravity of the offending, which is unfortunate but is to be preferred to the injustice of imposing a longer head sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: It might also be necessary to follow this approach if the offender has committed multiple serious offences, or where there are no exceptional circumstances and so concurrency is expressly precluded by s 16(3B) of the Act. The need to follow the secondary approach in this instance arises because the legislative preclusion does not exclude operation of the totality principle.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: There is conflicting authority on whether such interstate offending must be close in time and of a similar kind, so sentencing in such circumstances requires care.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: The totality principle also applies to fixing of the head sentence and the non-parole period, and it applies where the sentence currently being served derives from a breach of parole.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: The overall criminality is what must be assessed, and in most circumstances a court must consider what sentence would have been just and proper if all offences had fallen for sentencing on the same occasion.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: Instead, the prior sentences and time spent in custody simply remain part of an offender’s circumstances that must be considered to comply with the principle of totality.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: The totality principle applies when sentencing for offences that may overlap or be cumulated upon an existing custodial sentence. It applies not only to multiple sentences imposed at the same time, but to sentences imposed for offences committed on different occasions and in different States.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: The Court said that to the extent totality applies in such a case, it does so distinctly and not by considering the sentence that would have been imposed had all offending fallen for sentencing on the same occasion.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: But see Mendoza-Cortez v The Queen [2016] VSCA 302.
When applied to sentences imposed by a single court, totality may be achieved either by making sentences concurrent – wholly or in part – or by imposing disproportionately low terms.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: There are three reasons for the preferred approach. First, to ensure that each sentence appropriately reflects the criminality of each offence. Second, to ensure that if one or more sentence or conviction is set aside, that the remaining sentences will be appropriate and will allow a new total effective sentence and non-parole period to be calculated. And third, to avoid artificial claims of disparity by co-offenders aggrieved by the inadequate individual sentences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: It may be necessary to follow this approach in cases where the offender has previously served substantial periods of imprisonment and imposing conventional terms could result in a disproportionately long sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: ‘The totality principle is related to the proportionality principle’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: This might occur because the offender committed other offences before imprisonment that are only discovered later, because the offences took place in different jurisdictions, or because there were different victims.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: But in Sayer v The Queen, the Court of Appeal considered the case of an offender who had committed three separate rapes during three separate burglaries over five months in 1984 when he was 17 years old.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: By time he was charged and sentenced for the first offence in 2015, he had long since served full sentences for the second and third offences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

title: Totality and the serious offender provisions (ss 6D, 6E)
statement: Section 6D affects totality much as it affects proportionality: the court must be satisfied the offender will remain a danger beyond the period totality would permit. Section 6E makes cumulation presumptive for serious offenders; the court must not undermine that policy by applying totality as if the legislation did not exist (but see DPP (Vic) v VH, fn 473), and it is wrong to “direct otherwise” simply to achieve what totality would have required. Guidance on resolving the s 6E/totality tension is limited: as objective gravity increases so might the degree of cumulation, or the secondary (moderated individual sentences) approach may be used.

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has held that this section has substantially the same impact on totality as it does on proportionality because the sentencing court will have to be satisfied that the offender ‘will remain a danger to the community beyond the period that totality would permit’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

refs.q: Second, unless the court orders otherwise, s 6E of the Act makes cumulation the presumptive order for sentences imposed on serious offenders for serious offences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

refs.q: Therefore, a court needs to be careful not to undermine that legislative policy by applying the totality principle as if the legislation did not exist.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

refs.q: Specifically, ‘[i]t would be wrong to ‘direct otherwise’ simply in order to achieve what totality might have required in the absence of s 6E’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

refs.q: There is limited guidance for the courts on how to resolve this tension between s 6E and the principle of totality, but as the objective gravity of the total offending increases, so might the degree of cumulation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

refs.q: This will produce a total effective sentence that respects both the legislation and the principle, or, as with s 16(3B), the secondary approach of moderating individual sentences may be employed to give effect to the legislative intent while imposing a sentence that complies with the requirements of totality.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

refs.q: But see DPP (Vic) v VH (2004) 10 VR 234, 237 [10].
The totality principle interacts with State legislation in two ways beyond those discussed below in the parole context.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

refs.q: First, as noted, s 6D of the Act provides that in sentencing a serious offender the Supreme or County Court may impose a disproportionate sentence if it considers it necessary to protect the community.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

refs.q: The High Court has said, with respect to the predecessor provision of s 6E, that the legislation gives effect to a policy that serious offenders are to be treated differently, and that if its operation were subject to the full effect of the totality principle its object would be compromised and defeated in most cases.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

title: Totality and offending on parole: s 5(2AA), cancellation, s 16(3B) and the “whole sentence”
statement: For totality, s 5(2AA) bars considering whether custody will be affected by executive action — e.g. whether parole might be granted at the end of the non-parole period (in fixing the non-parole period itself, 8.3.3.2 lets the court consider the possibility of release on parole: npp.no_executive_speculation; flag.parole_consideration_3_3_3_vs_8_3_3_2). Because it is prospective, it bars totality only where parole has not been revoked at sentence; once revoked (including automatic cancellation under the Corrections Act — s 77(6) “on conviction” for listed offences committed on parole for such an offence; s 77(7A) at the time of sentencing when a prison sentence is imposed for parole offending), the whole sentence may be considered. A long line of Court of Appeal cases held that only the additional period the offender must serve because of the cancellation was considered; Koumis held that the entire period imposed for the prior offending (the time served before release on parole and the balance after cancellation) should be considered, and DPP v Bowen affirmed that view — so that the combined effect is not disproportionate to the aggregated criminality. Under s 16(3B), absent exceptional circumstances, sentences for offending on parole are cumulative on the period served because of cancellation (the offender normally serves the balance first), and totality must not be applied inconsistently with that intention — but viewed as a whole the terms cannot exceed what totality and the purposes require; neither the head sentence nor the non-parole period for the later offences may be disproportionate to the total criminality (the further statement that “the parole sentence has no role to play” beyond that rests on Dickson and Waugh, from the line Bowen overtook: caution, flag.parole_no_role_rests_on_disapproved_line). “Exceptional circumstances” is a relative and protean concept; re-offending on parole from a life sentence has been held exceptional (warranting concurrency), without precluding cumulation among the later offences. If parole has not been cancelled at sentence, no s 16(3B) order can be made without breaching s 5(2AA) (when that case arises once s 77(7A) operates is unclear: flag.parole_not_cancelled_at_sentence). Totality is significant but not controlling.

refs.q: Specifically, s 5(2AA) prohibits a sentencing court from considering the possibility or likelihood that the length of time spent in custody ‘will be affected by executive action of any kind’. In other words, a sentencing court should not consider whether the offender might be granted parole at the expiration of the non-parole period, either in Victoria or in another jurisdiction.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: But it has been held that this creates an anomalous situation because by its use of the prospective language – ‘will be’ – s 5(2AA) precludes application of the totality principle only if parole has not been revoked at the time of sentencing. If parole has already been revoked by that date, a court is not precluded from applying the principle.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: These provisions do not require speculation about future executive action, cancellation is a fait accompli and so the ‘whole sentence’ an offender must serve as the result of their parole cancellation may be considered.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: That minority view was affirmed in DPP (Vic) v Bowen where a full bench of five judges said that when a breach of parole is involved, totality requires the court to consider two sentences: the one to be imposed for the breach, and the original sentence imposed for the prior offending. The sentencing court must be satisfied that the combined effect of the two is not ‘disproportionate to the aggregated criminality involved in the breach offending and the prior offending’. In doing so, it is the entire period of time served that should be considered.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: Section 16(3B) of the Act further directs that absent a finding of exceptional circumstances, every sentence imposed for offending committed while on parole must be served cumulatively on any period an offender must serve as the result of their parole having been cancelled.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: The obvious intention behind this section is that in cases where an offender has committed a crime while on parole they will normally first be required to serve the balance of the earlier term. A court must give effect to this intention and must not apply the principle of totality to the extent that it is inconsistent.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: Absent exceptional circumstances, there must be cumulation with respect to offences committed while on parole, but ‘viewed as a whole’ the aggregate terms also cannot be greater than what is needed to fulfil the totality principle and the sentencing purposes.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: As the Court of Appeal explained in R v Hunter, ‘[t]here must be relativity between the totality of the criminality and the totality of sentences, not only for the offences for which the person is being sentenced, but for the sentence which the person is currently serving’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: The sentencing court must be satisfied that neither the head sentence nor the non-parole period fixed for the later offences is disproportionate to the total criminality represented by both the later offences and the original offences. ‘Beyond that, however, the parole sentence has no role to play in the sentencing for the later offences’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: What constitutes ‘exceptional circumstances’ for the purposes of s 16(3B) is a ‘relative and protean’ concept that requires ‘a determination of fact and degree on the basis of the facts and circumstances of the case in issue’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has found that where an offender re-offends while on parole for a life sentence this is an exceptional circumstance and warrants the imposition of a concurrent term. But this does not preclude cumulation between later offences if the total effective sentence for them is ordered to be served concurrently with the cancelled parole sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: The court must fix appropriate sentences to reflect the criminality of the parole offending and the totality principle has limited operation in relation to the existing sentence of life imprisonment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: Note that unlike cases where parole has been cancelled prior to sentencing for the offences committed on parole, where parole has not been cancelled at the time of sentencing, the court may not make an order pursuant to s 16(3B) for cumulation or concurrency without breaching s 5(2AA).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: Lastly, to say that totality is significant when parole is cancelled and in aggregating a term for the later offending is not to say that the principle becomes controlling, and it is wrong to assume the offender being ordered to serve further time in custody will offend totality.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: Section 77(6) of which provides that when a person commits a sexual offence, a serious violent offence, a terrorism offence, or a foreign incursion offence while on parole for an earlier such offence, the earlier parole is taken to have been cancelled ‘on conviction’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: Similarly, s 77(7A) provides that if a prisoner is sentenced to another prison sentence for an offence committed on parole, whether in Victoria or elsewhere, the parole is taken to have been cancelled at the time of sentencing for the subsequent offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: In a long line of cases, the Court of Appeal held this meant that only the additional period the offender is required to serve as the result of their parole being cancelled must be considered.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: But in Koumis v The Queen the Court held the entire period imposed for prior offending, i.e., the period served before release on parole and the balance to be served following cancellation of parole, should be considered when sentencing for subsequent offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: Further informing this limitation are the automatic cancellation provisions of the Corrections Act 1986 (Vic).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: Totality concerns are important when sentencing an offender for crimes committed while on parole.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: This is because the Act partially limits the principle’s application.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

refs.q: What comprises a ‘whole sentence’ was the subject of conflicting authority.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

title: Totality and crushing sentences are different tests
statement: A crushing sentence does not inherently offend totality; the two are not the same, and a sentence may offend totality without being crushing — although some authority treats avoiding a crushing sentence as a very significant part, or the second limb, of the totality analysis (fn 502; flag.crushing_within_totality).

refs.q: A crushing sentence is not one that inherently offends the principle of totality. They are not the same and a sentence may offend totality without being crushing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.4 – Interaction with the other principles

refs.q: But see Mohamed v The Queen [2022] VSCA 136, [77] (stating that the need to avoid a crushing sentence is ‘a very significant part of the totality analysis’), quoting DPP (Vic) v Alsop [2010] VSCA 325, [30] (indicating that the need to avoid a crushing sentence is the second limb of the totality principle).

title: Double punishment: the test
statement: Punishment should reflect only what the offender did, not how offence boundaries are drawn: an offender may be prosecuted for conduct constituting several offences but not punished more than once for the same act or omission. The enquiry is one of common sense, not semantics. A wholly subsumed offence should not be sentenced at all, even concurrently. A single act causing separate harms (especially to different people) may be punished separately, and some cumulation may be called for where one action constitutes two distinct harms. The test is whether one sentence includes an element of punishment also included in another; with no common elements or facts, no question arises. An aggregate sentence is unlikely to raise the risk. The area is complex and hard to reduce to firm guidelines.

refs.q: The punishment should reflect only what the offender has done, not the way the legislative boundaries of crimes have been drawn. The boundaries of different offences often overlap and punishing someone twice for conduct that falls within the overlapping area does not punish only for what the person deserves.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: It is permissible to prosecute a person for acts or omissions that may constitute more than one offence, but it is not permissible to punish them ‘more than once for the same act or omission’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: The enquiry must be approached as a matter of common sense, not as a matter of semantics.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment
