refs.q: If the elements of one offence are wholly subsumed within another, then an offender should not be sentenced for the subsumed offence, not even if the sentence is made entirely concurrent with the primary sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: But where a single act reflects separate harms, particularly separate harms against different people, each may be punished separately, even when linked by time and place.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: An appropriate measure of cumulation may also be called for where a single action constitutes two distinct harms. The test is whether in the process of arriving at sentences for overlapping offending, a court includes in one sentence an element of punishment that is also included in the other.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: ‘Where there are no elements or factual matters common to two or more of the counts no question of double punishment will arise’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: The risk of double punishment is not likely to arise when an aggregate sentence is imposed because in doing so a court is considering the offender’s whole conduct and there is no overlapping criminality.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: This area of sentencing law is complex and ambiguous.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: The rule against double punishment derives from both legislation and the common law.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: Identifying a single act as common to two offences can be difficult.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

title: Double punishment: further examples by offence type
statement: Further worked examples from 3.4.1–3.4.7 for checking multi-charge structures (see each example’s quotes). Each is a decided case, not a general rule: the Manual says the area is complex and ambiguous, and several examples carry contrary authority (fns 526, 530, 549), so (app policy) a borderline structure is a caution, not an error.

examples.text: Separate penetrations in one continuing transaction may call for substantial concurrency; an abduction sentence explicable only by the rape it led to doubly punishes; cumulating breaches of supervision orders on the sentences for the offences constituting them does not.

refs.q: But it has also held that rapes involving two separate penetrations were effectively part of a single continuing transaction that called for substantial concurrency.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.1 – Sex offences

refs.q: Similarly, a sentence of four years’ and six months’ imprisonment for an offence of abduction with the intent to take part in an act of sexual penetration, of which two years and six months was cumulated on an 11-year term imposed for rape, was held to doubly punish the accused.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.1 – Sex offences

refs.q: Some cumulation was considered appropriate, but the sentence ‘was so high as to be explicable only on the basis that the sentencing judge must have been influenced, when assessing the gravity of the abduction, by what the abduction led to, namely, the rape itself’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.1 – Sex offences

refs.q: However, cumulating sentences for breaches of an interim extended supervision order and an extended supervision order upon sentences for the sexual offences that comprise the acts constituting the breaches does not doubly punish the offender because failing to comply with the supervision orders involves the added criminality of failing to comply with orders of the court.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.1 – Sex offences

examples.text: Where a single actus reus (firing a pistol) underlay reckless conduct endangering, recklessly causing injury and prohibited-person firearm use, sentencing for all three doubly punished (R v Le); but a nearly identical single action (firing a shotgun) may breach two distinct offences and call for some cumulation (Phillips17), and arson and recklessly causing serious injury do not necessarily share an actus reus (BBA). Not a general rule: fn 526 records the contrary authority.

refs.q: For example, where offending has a single actus reus, such as the firing of a pistol, it would doubly punish an offender to sentence them for reckless conduct placing another in danger of serious injury, recklessly causing injury, and being a prohibited person using an unregistered firearm.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.2 – Harm to/Endangering the person

refs.q: But see Phillips17 [43]–[44] where the Court said the nearly identical single action, firing a shotgun, may breach the legal obligations imposed by two distinct offences — recklessly causing injury and reckless conduct engendering serious injury — and so call for an appropriate measure of cumulation.
See also BBA v The Queen [2010] VSCA 174, [38] (holding that arson and recklessly cause serious injury do not necessarily involve the same actus reus and so some cumulation may be appropriate).

examples.text: Trafficking is an aggravated form of possession; possession of cannabis harvested from a cultivated crop overlaps the cultivation; theft of electricity adds to cultivation (some cumulation); possession of a precursor differs from possessing materials for trafficking (but concurrency may be ordered where one is subsumed); conspiracy to import and attempting to possess an imported drug are separate criminality. Two trafficking charges for different drugs from a single business may share commonalities (Dang), but see Nguyen (fn 530: not double punishment where two drugs were combined in one tablet).

refs.q: Approaching it from a common-sense perspective, a count of trafficking is essentially an aggravated form of the offence of possession; thus counts of possessing a traffickable quantity and a commercial quantity merely charge an offender with possession simpliciter of some quantity of the drug they are charged with trafficking. These are essentially the same criminal acts for which an offender cannot be doubly punished.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.3 – Drugs

refs.q: Similarly, it is double punishment to sentence for possession of cannabis and cultivating a commercial quantity of cannabis where the possessed cannabis was harvested from that which was cultivated.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.3 – Drugs

refs.q: But although the theft of electricity may be an important part of the enterprise of cultivating commercial quantities of cannabis, it is different and adds to the cultivation offence by concealing it and making it more profitable. Therefore, some period of cumulation is appropriate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.3 – Drugs

refs.q: Possession of a precursor chemical is also different in character from possessing substances, materials or equipment for trafficking because the legal elements are different, and the latter offending requires a specific intent that the former does not.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.3 – Drugs

refs.q: Nonetheless, if it is possible for a jury to reason ‘that the act constituting possession of the precursor chemical in no less than the prescribed quantity was subsumed within the charge of possession of a substance with the intent of using it to traffick in a drug of dependence’, then a court may order concurrency between the terms to avoid double punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.3 – Drugs

refs.q: Lastly, an offence of conspiracy to import a marketable quantity of a border-controlled drug, with an admission that at least one overt, but unidentified, act has been committed pursuant to the conspiracy, is not the same as attempting to possess a marketable quantity of an unlawfully imported border-controlled drug.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.3 – Drugs

refs.q: See also Dang v The Queen [2014] VSCA 49 which held that two Giretti charges of trafficking in methylaphetamine and heroin resulting from a single business of selling drugs have commonalities that are not distinguished by the different narcotics trafficked. But see Nguyen v The Queen [2011] VSCA 139, [15] where, although the accused similarly trafficked two separate drugs, ecstasy and cocaine, the Court said that sentencing for both is not double punishment despite the two being combined in one tablet.

examples.text: Cumulative fines for summary driving offences may doubly punish where conduct overlaps; a PCA offence does not overlap reckless or dangerous driving; failing to stop and failing to render assistance cover essentially the same conduct.

refs.q: Fines imposed for the summary offences of driving under the influence and speeding, which are cumulative on sentences for negligently causing serious injury, may doubly punish an offender if there is overlap between the criminal conduct that underlies the convictions.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.4 – Driving offences

refs.q: But a sentence imposed for the summary offence of driving while exceeding the prescribed concentration of alcohol does not doubly punish an offender cumulatively sentenced for reckless or dangerous driving causing serious injury. This is because the summary offence occurs as soon as the driver takes charge of their car and it is not an element of reckless or dangerous driving.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.4 – Driving offences

refs.q: Therefore, it is not double punishment to cumulate sentences in such cases.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.4 – Driving offences

refs.q: However, failing to stop after an accident causing serious injury and failing to render assistance after an accident cover ‘essentially the same conduct’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.4 – Driving offences

examples.text: Possessing an item to damage property and arson with intent to endanger life on overlapping facts.

refs.q: Where the prosecution contends that the facts underlying a charge of possessing an item with the intention of using it to damage property also partly underlie a charge of intentionally damaging premises by fire with the intent to endanger life, it would be artificial to justify punishment on both charges.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.5 – Property damage

examples.text: Aggravated burglary is complete on entry (later events still relevant); weapon possession on entry and its later use; false-document counts over several days may be one transaction; deception and dealing with proceeds may overlap.

refs.q: Separating the bases of punishment in cases where several offences are committed within a single incident is complicated where one of the offences is aggravated burglary, and care must be taken in sentencing for that crime to ensure an accused is not doubly punished.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.6 – Theft/Fraud

refs.q: But this does not mean that events occurring after entry are irrelevant to the sentencing process; their effect on the sentence depends on the circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.6 – Theft/Fraud

refs.q: The court must be careful not to doubly punish the offender for both possessing a weapon at the time of entry and then using that weapon when committing offences within the premises.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.6 – Theft/Fraud

refs.q: Multiple counts of using false documents for fraudulent purposes may not be separate transactions, even if they occurred over different days. The use of the documents might be the actus reus of each count and make cumulation of the sentences an error.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.6 – Theft/Fraud

refs.q: Similarly, attempting to obtain financial advantage by deception and dealing with the proceeds of crime are different offences with separate and distinct elements, but there may be considerable overlap if the dealing with proceeds charge involves using them to conceal the earlier attempts.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.6 – Theft/Fraud

examples.text: Use of a firearm in the principal offence and possession by a prohibited person need moderation (but see Robinson, fn 549: a degree of cumulation reflecting the different culpability of prohibited-person possession and possession as an element of aggravated burglary is permissible); a separately charged firearm-carrying offence may be punished and aggravate the principal offence without double punishment.

refs.q: When an offender is sentenced for offending that is aggravated by using a firearm and for being a prohibited person in possession of an unregistered firearm, the sentence for the possession charge cannot include any penalty for the use or possession of the weapon in the first offending without moderating the sentences to account for double punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.7 – Weapons offences

refs.q: In Victoria, offences that involve use of a weapon include: • causing serious injury intentionally in circumstances of gross violence; • causing serious injury recklessly in circumstances of gross violence; • using a firearm to resist arrest; • being armed with criminal intent; • armed robbery; • aggravated burglary; • home invasion; • aggravated home invasion; • aggravated carjacking; and • dangerous goods on an aircraft.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.7 – Weapons offences

refs.q: Similarly, if the offending was committed while the accused carried a firearm, that is a separate offence which may be both punished itself and considered as aggravating the principle offence, so long as it is separately charged, and the sentence imposed does not double punish the accused, whether via cumulation or otherwise.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.7 – Weapons offences

refs.q: But see Robinson v The Queen [2017] VSCA 304, [27]–[35] (‘Robinson’) where the Court said that a degree of cumulation reflecting the different criminal culpability associated with being a prohibited person possessing a firearm and possessing a firearm as an element of the offence of aggravated burglary is permissible and does not doubly punish the offender.
The double punishment principle has been applied in varied circumstances with varied outcomes for which it is hard to formulate firm guidelines.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment

refs.q: Driving offences often raise a risk of double punishment, particularly if summary offences are charged.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.4 – Driving offences

refs.q: Continuing transactions and combined events are prominent features of dishonesty offences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.6 – Theft/Fraud

refs.q: Property offences involving weapons also pose challenges for the principle of double punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.4 – Double punishment > 3.4.6 – Theft/Fraud

title: Crushing sentences: what the principle is, and is not
statement: There is no principle that a crushing sentence must be avoided: it is an expression of the principle that a sentence should promote rehabilitation where possible, and in grave cases little weight can be given to rehabilitation. It is wrong to set a minimum by the need to ensure “some measure of life after release”. Age (advanced or youthful) may be significant but cannot support an inappropriate sentence. Extreme length alone does not make a sentence crushing, and there are no hard and fast rules. An offender may by their crimes forfeit the expectation of a useful life after release, and community protection may justify a sentence the offender sees as crushing (s 6D may produce one: purpose.community_protection_detail). A crushing term is of greater concern for older offenders. The authority for the “no principle” statement (fn 564) is incomplete in the Manual (flag.citation_incomplete_fn564). The Manual also says a court should not impose a crushing sentence unless there are special circumstances (principle.crushing_sentence; the two statements: flag.crushing_sentence_principle).

refs.q: But there is no sentencing principle that requires a crushing sentence to be avoided. It is a particular expression of the principle that wherever possible a sentence should be imposed to promote the rehabilitation of the offender and there will be occasions when the offending is so grave that little weight can be given in the sentencing calculus to promoting the offender’s rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: It is wrong, however, to determine a minimum sentence by the need to ensure ‘some measure of life after release’. This approach may lead to an impermissible disregard of the circumstances and the other sentencing factors.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: However, while age (advanced or youthful) is a factor to be considered, and may even be a significant factor, it cannot support the imposition of an inappropriate sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: Nor does the extreme length of a sentence by itself justify the label of ‘crushing’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: There are no ‘hard and fast rules’ for deciding when the totality of the sentences is crushing. That depends on the facts but is informed by the nature and circumstances of all the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: In other words, there will be cases where an offender has, by their criminal act(s), forfeited the right to expect they will be released from confinement with a useful period of their lifetime left to enjoy. The need to protect the community is also a significant consideration and may similarly justify a sentence that an offender might view as crushing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: Obviously, the imposition of a ‘crushing’ term is of greater concern to older offenders, since their age and a lengthy term of imprisonment increases the likelihood of their having little useful life left upon release.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

title: Parity: scope, comparison and how to apply it
statement: Parity is an aspect of equal justice (like treated alike) but does not require strict comparison or the same sentence. The court must assess the individuals and circumstances; a comparative analysis of culpability is indispensable. Co-offenders are preferably sentenced together by the same judge; otherwise the later judge should learn the earlier sentence and its circumstances. A substantial discount to one offender must be considered for the other and may require some reduction, but an excessively lenient sentence cannot justify an inappropriately low one. Further justified differences include gender-related burdens (not gender itself), an agreed statement of facts, and positive participation in the Koori Court with a year under its supervision. Parity applies to all co-offenders (not just the lowest sentence) and to everyone in a common criminal enterprise (but see Huu, fn 605) (participants need not act at the same time or know of each other). Related offending may be relevant, weighted by nexus, similarity and personal factors; a sufficient nexus may require close conformity even without a common enterprise. Parity is harder to apply as the crimes differ. Percentages of non-parole periods and head sentences may help. Parity may require a substantially lower penalty. A common criminal enterprise is a course of criminal activity of multiple unlawful acts of the same or similar nature, related to the same criminal purpose. If co-offenders are not sentenced together, an appellate court is not justified in interfering on parity grounds on that account (fn 581). For adult and juvenile co-offenders parity has only a limited application, but the youthful offender’s sentence remains part of the background for the adult.

refs.q: It is an aspect of equal justice which, traditionally put, requires that like be treated alike.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: But this does not mean ‘that sentences must strictly compare’ or that co-offenders must receive the same sentence for the same offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: There is no scientifically precise way to quantify disparities between offenders.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: The court must assess the individuals and the circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: A comparative analysis of the culpability and circumstances of co-offenders is indispensable to application of the parity principle.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: To facilitate that analysis the strong preference is for all co-offenders to be sentenced by the same judge at the same time, and where this is not possible the judge imposing the later sentence should inform themselves of the sentence already imposed and its circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: If a substantial discount is given to one offender, parity requires that their sentence – even if regarded as manifestly too low – be considered in sentencing the co-offender and may also require some reduction in that sentence. But an excessively lenient sentence cannot justify the reduction of a co-offender’s sentence to an inappropriately low level.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: • by significant differences associated with gender – for example, the increased burden of imprisonment on the mother of a young child, even though gender itself does not justify a differential sentence;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: • between an offender sentenced per an agreed statement of facts and one who has not had that benefit.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: • when an offender participates positively in the Koori Court and is under its supervision for a year.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Parity applies to all co-offenders (there cannot be a comparison to only the lowest sentence passed on a single co-offender), and to all people involved in a common criminal enterprise.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: But they do not need to have participated at the same time or have known of the other’s participation in similar acts.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: The weight given to the comparative sentence will depend on ‘the nexus between the offenders, the degree of similarity between their conduct, and factors personal to each offender’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Even when there is no common criminal enterprise, if there is a sufficient nexus between and important common features of the offending, the principles of parity and consistency may become so closely related to the principle of equal justice that the sentence imposed on one offender may be required to closely conform to that imposed on another offender for a related crime.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: But parity becomes more difficult to apply as differences in the nature and seriousness between the crimes charged become greater.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: In assessing whether disparity is justified, it may be useful to compare the respective non-parole periods and head sentences of co-offenders in percentage terms.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Parity may even require the imposition of a penalty substantially less than what might otherwise be imposed because it is a ‘fundamental requirement of justice and the rule of law’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: A common criminal enterprise involves a course of criminal activity involving multiple unlawful acts of the same or similar nature, all related to the same criminal purpose.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: But if this does not occur, an appellate court is not justified in interfering in the sentencing process on parity grounds.
Again, however, the sentence imposed on the youthful offender remains part of the background to be considered in sentencing the adult offender;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Parity is recognised by statute and the common law.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Its purpose is to ensure consistency in punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: As the Court of Appeal put it in Ah-Kau v The Queen, ‘ultimately, it is an evaluation based on impression’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: The courts have found that disparate sentencing may be justified:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: The different offenders will have all participated in the enterprise at some point, which establishes the necessary relationship or association between them.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: There will usually be one continuous participant throughout the enterprise.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: If the offending is very similar and is in some way related, the sentence imposed on one offender may be relevant in sentencing another.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: The same victim or subject matter might be involved, or there may be some other connection.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: This is, of course, a discretionary decision to be made in all the circumstances of the case.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: It may reach a point where the principle can no longer be applied and there are limits upon which a court may compare sentences of people charged with different crimes.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

title: Parity on appeal: Crown appeals, re-sentencing and co-appellants
statement: Parity arguments have very little chance of success where the co-offenders were sentenced for multiple counts, or where one was sentenced for several counts and the other for only one. The DPP may appeal only one co-offender’s sentence. Normally, given the limited and specific nature of a Crown appeal, the court is constrained from intervening even if it considers the sentence manifestly inadequate; parity may limit intervention but does not require the court to decline to intervene; on re-sentence the co-offender’s sentence must be taken into account, but parity cannot require a wholly inappropriate sentence. Parity is relevant to the residual discretion, which the court may decline to exercise where giving full weight to parity would produce unjustifiable disparity amounting to an affront to justice. A reduction for one appellant re-opens the discretion for co-offenders who appealed, without requiring a reduction.

refs.q: Parity arguments also have very little chance of success on appeal if the co-offenders have been sentenced for multiple counts, or where one offender is sentenced for several counts and the other offender for only one count.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: Parity does not preclude the Director from appealing against only one sentence in a case involving two or more offenders. The principle does not require that an appeal be taken from the sentences of all or both.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: However, parity does not ‘so circumscribe[] the sentencing discretion as to require the Court to decline to intervene’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: If an appellate court determines the sentence was manifestly inadequate and re-sentences the offender, then as with an offender’s appeal, the sentence imposed on their co-offender(s) must be taken into account by the appeals court to minimise any disparity created by the new sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: Although this can be done by increasing the sentence to the lower range of adequate sentences, parity with the co-offender’s sentence cannot require imposing a new sentence that is wholly inappropriate or disproportionate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: Considerations of parity are also relevant to an appellate court’s exercise of the residual discretion in a Director’s appeal.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: If the sentence of an offender is reduced on appeal, parity requires the sentencing discretion be re-opened for all co-offenders who have appealed against their sentence. It does not, however, require that a reduced sentence then be imposed on them.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: Normally, given the limited and specific nature of a Crown appeal, the court is constrained from intervening even if it considers sentence to be manifestly inadequate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: However, a court may decline to exercise the discretion where giving full weight to parity considerations would lead to unjustifiable disparity that would be an affront to justice.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: Specifically, parity may act as a limiting factor when only one of several sentences is challenged: ‘In such circumstances a sentence which is regarded as inadequate might still be permitted to stand’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: An appellate court will rarely re-sentence based on disparity because sentencing is imprecise and involves an exercise of judicial discretion respecting conflicting principles that ‘will almost inevitably produce disparity between sentences imposed, even in the case of co-offenders’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

title: Totality: shortcuts and impression
statement: Problems arise when shortcuts are adopted (e.g. fixing a single term for Commonwealth offences to be served before a State term commences risks not reflecting the totality of the Commonwealth offending). Whether totality is offended is often a matter of impression, subsumed in manifest excess or inadequacy. (app policy) State the individual sentences and the cumulation steps rather than jumping to a total.
note: jurisdiction mixed: the shortcut example concerns Commonwealth and State terms together (Commonwealth sentencing is outside the app’s scope); the impression point applies generally.

refs.q: Problems with the application of totality arise when shortcuts are adopted to give effect to the principle.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.5 – Challenges in application

refs.q: But determining whether the principle of totality has been offended is often – like manifest excess – a matter of impression, which follows since complaints about totality are subsumed within complaints about manifest excess or inadequacy.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.5 – Challenges in application

refs.q: For example: fixing a single term of imprisonment to be served for Commonwealth offences before the commencement of a term for State offences, carries an appreciable risk that the sentence will not adequately reflect the totality of the offending on the Commonwealth charges.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.5 – Challenges in application

refs.q: This approach is a problematic ‘short cut’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.5 – Challenges in application

title: Totality in Commonwealth sentencing (outside the app’s Victorian scope)
statement: State sentencing gives effect to totality by concurrency and cumulation; Commonwealth sentencing by commencement dates (Cth Crimes Act s 16B — the court must consider any unserved sentence and any sentence liable to be served because of a revocation of parole; common law on concurrency).

refs.q: In State sentencing the primary manner for effecting the totality principle is by tailoring orders for concurrency and cumulation. In Commonwealth sentencing this is accomplished by imposing different commencement dates.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.2 – Commonwealth

refs.q: The Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) s 16B (‘Cth Crimes Act’) also implicitly recognises the totality principle by providing that a sentencing court ‘must’ consider any sentence already imposed on a person that they have not served and any sentence they are liable to serve because of a revocation of parole.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.2 – Commonwealth

title: Parity on appeal: marked disparity and a justifiable sense of grievance
statement: Disparity on appeal is approached like manifest excess; intervention needs disparity so marked as to produce a legitimate and justifiable sense of grievance in the objective observer (i.e. the differential was not reasonably open). Parity arguments rarely succeed where the co-offenders were sentenced for multiple counts, or where one was sentenced for several counts and the other for only one. In Crown appeals parity may limit intervention, but does not require a wholly inappropriate sentence. If one offender’s sentence is reduced, the discretion reopens for appealing co-offenders, without requiring a reduction.

refs.q: On appeal, disparity in the treatment of co-offenders is approached with the same analytical framework as manifest excess.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: Therefore, appellate intervention requires the disparity (or lack) to be so ‘marked’ or ‘manifest’ that it will ‘produce a legitimate and justifiable sense of grievance in the objective observer’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: A justifiable sense of grievance does not refer to the offender’s subjective state of mind, it means that a ‘sentencing differential’ was not reasonably open.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: Parity arguments also have very little chance of success on appeal if the co-offenders have been sentenced for multiple counts, or where one offender is sentenced for several counts and the other offender for only one count.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: Although this can be done by increasing the sentence to the lower range of adequate sentences, parity with the co-offender’s sentence cannot require imposing a new sentence that is wholly inappropriate or disproportionate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

refs.q: If the sentence of an offender is reduced on appeal, parity requires the sentencing discretion be re-opened for all co-offenders who have appealed against their sentence. It does not, however, require that a reduced sentence then be imposed on them.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity > 3.6.1 – Appeals

title: Weighing the purposes: they overlap and may point in different directions
statement: Sentencing is difficult because each purpose must be given appropriate weight, and the purposes overlap and cannot be considered in isolation. More than one purpose is often furthered, and which (if any) is paramount depends on all the circumstances and is a matter for the court’s discretion.

refs.q: But sentencing remains a difficult exercise because of the need to give appropriate weight to each of the purposes, which overlap and cannot be considered in isolation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: More than one purpose may be (and often is) furthered by a given sentence, and determining which purpose, if any, is paramount depends on all circumstances and is a discretionary matter for the sentencing court.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: The purposes were developed by the courts out of the need to promote consistency in sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes

title: Just punishment and denunciation: content and limits
statement: Retribution does not mean “an eye for an eye”: the court recognises what accords with the moral sense of the community, and the law must be administered in a way the community can understand and regard as fair and just. Determining a just sentence is not mechanical, and guidelines for the synthesis cannot be set without impeding the discretion. Denunciation communicates, through the type or duration of the sentence, society’s condemnation of the conduct; the court speaks with reference to community expectations and values and must vindicate them and be seen to do so. The sentence must acknowledge the personal damage to the victim (whose rehabilitation may be harder than the offender’s). Denunciation and retribution have less relevance for an offender with a mental disability who cannot appreciate the condemnation; an intelligent offender whose conduct is a deliberate affront cannot expect leniency. For a youthful offender, rehabilitation must give way in crimes of great gravity or violence, and significantly so for an intended terrorist act.

refs.q: It is more accurate, however, to say that retribution does not require ‘an eye for an eye’ but requires a court to recognise what accords with ‘the moral sense of the community’ when imposing sentence. The criminal law must be administered in a way that can be understood by the community and regarded by it as complying with what it considers ‘fair and just’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: But determining a just sentence is not a mechanical exercise. The impact of the factors will vary from case to case, with no one factor controlling. It is not possible to set guidelines for the synthesis without impeding the court’s discretion to fix a just penalty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: It requires a sentence to communicate – through its type or duration – society’s condemnation and disapproval of the conduct; it is a collective statement that the offender’s conduct should be punished for encroaching on society’s basic values as embodied in the criminal law.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: In denouncing an offender’s conduct, a court should speak with reference to community expectations and values. The courts are part of the community and may be viewed as the trustees of the community’s power to judge and punish. This means they must vindicate the values of the community and be seen to be doing so.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: The sentence imposed must acknowledge the personal damage done to the victim and that their rehabilitation may actually be far more difficult than the offender’s.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: For example: the retributive effect and denunciatory aspect of a sentence have less relevance to a mentally disabled offender who is incapable of appreciating the societal condemnation of the sentence, nor would the community likely demand that an individual with such lessened moral culpability be severely punished.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: Conversely, an offender of intelligence and ability whose conduct might be taken as a deliberate affront to society’s expectations cannot expect leniency.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: Similarly, while rehabilitation is frequently said to be the predominant purpose in sentencing a youthful offender, there are crimes of such gravity or violence that rehabilitation must give way to the requirements of just punishment and denunciation. In particular, the Court of Appeal has said rehabilitation must give way, significantly, to the need for a sentence to adequately express the court’s and the community’s repugnance at an intended terrorist act.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: Public denunciation is a logically related fundamental purpose.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: Older cases refer to these purposes as ‘retribution’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: At its basest, retribution is said to punish the offender ‘because they deserve it’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: Public denunciation of the offending conduct and reinforcement of society’s expectations is a central purpose of sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

refs.q: It ‘serves to reinforce the standards which society expects its members to observe’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.1 – Just punishment and denunciation

title: Deterrence: no non-parole period, and impairment arising after the offending
statement: Where imprisonment is imposed with no minimum term, deterrence is given the most weight; if deterrence predominates it may, rarely, be appropriate to make little or no allowance for mitigating factors. A mental impairment or illness that develops after the offending may require moderation of general and specific deterrence: the court asks, at sentence, whether the offender is an “appropriate vehicle” for deterrence (the offender should not be used as a model for others) — but not where the condition resulted from the discovery of the crime and fear of a long prison term (the offender is the author of their predicament). Deterrence may be less relevant where the offender is motivated by an ideology or religion that calls for martyrdom (but see MHK, fn 672).

refs.q: When a term of imprisonment is imposed, and no minimum term is fixed, deterrence is being given the most weight, and if deterrence is the predominant purpose, it may, in rare instances, be appropriate to make little or no allowance for mitigating factors in determining the appropriate sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: Moderation of general and specific deterrence may be required if the offender develops a mental impairment or illness after the offending. If so, at the date of sentencing the court will need to determine if, because of the illness or impairment, the offender is not an ‘appropriate vehicle’ for deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: A reduction is not required, however, where the condition has arisen as a result of the crime’s discovery and the offender’s reaction to the possibility of a long prison term.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: The reason deterrence is moderated where the illness or impairment developed after, but not as a result of discovering, the offending is because the offender should not be used as a model for others.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: But where the discovery of the offending caused the condition, that view is moderated because the offender ‘is the author of their own predicament’ and may serve as a deterrent to others.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: Deterrence, general and specific, may also be less relevant where the offender is motivated by ideology or belief in a religion that calls for martyrdom.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: But see MHK.
In these circumstances the community would not expect the same penalty to be imposed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: The community will also not expect a lesser penalty to be imposed because an offender has a bad reaction to the discovery of their crime(s) and fears imprisonment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

refs.q: They are then analogous to someone with a gambling or substance addiction, who has contributed in part to their own condition and is still subject to deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence

title: General deterrence: how it operates and where its weight changes
statement: General deterrence depends on community awareness of sentences; if outcomes are not known they lose their deterrent effect (courts rely on the media and government to communicate them). It imposes a severity the offender’s criminality does not itself warrant, so it must not cause injustice; it has separately contributed only if the sentence was increased above what specific deterrence alone would justify. It must not be used to target a specific ethnic community. It is important in familial offending (a person should be able to leave a relationship without fear), and of paramount concern for offending in custody. For an elderly offender it is considered in light of the greater burden of prison and public perception. It is significant regardless of provocation or motive. It has minimal relevance when sentencing a child, and the matters in CYFA s 362(1) preclude it from being considered when a child is sentenced under that Act; it is unclear whether it applies where charges that might have been dealt with in the Children’s Court are dealt with in a superior court — it likely applies if punishment beyond that Act (or s 32(3)(b)) is needed (flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges). For youthful offenders rehabilitation is usually more important, but not automatically: in murder there is much less room for youth, and where a youthful offender carries out or plans extreme violence, youth is diminished quite substantially in weighing general deterrence. For an adult sentenced for offending committed as a child, its weight depends on multiple factors, including the seriousness of the offence and offending, remorse and rehabilitation prospects; where general deterrence is a significant purpose there is less scope for leniency based on youth.

refs.q: If sentencing outcomes are not known to the community, they will lose their deterrent effect.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: A significant problem is that as the courts are poorly equipped to communicate the sentence, the media and government must assist.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: A sentence is imposed in the hope that its severity, which the extent of an offender’s criminality does not of itself warrant, ‘will temper the criminal tendencies of others’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: For general deterrence to be considered to have separately contributed to a sentence, the sentence must have been increased, because of the need to send a deterrent message to others, above the sentence that would otherwise have been appropriate if specific deterrence alone was taken into account.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: Similarly, while an offender’s case and sentence are used as the vehicle for general deterrence, care must be taken to ensure that general deterrence is not used to target a specific ethnic community.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: General deterrence is important where offences are committed in a familial context because a person should be able to leave a relationship without fear of reprisal.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: Finally, it is of paramount concern for offending committed in a custodial setting because the victim, in part, has no choice but to be where they are and because the courts cannot permit ‘the law of the jungle to take hold in prisons’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: It must be considered in light of the effect imposing a jail sentence on elderly person will have on public perception, given the sentence will be more burdensome for that offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: The Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 (Vic) s 362(1) lists the matters that must be taken into account when sentencing. The nature of the matters referred to in that section preclude general deterrence from being considered when sentencing child offenders pursuant to that Act.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: It is likely the deterrent purpose will apply if a court decides that punishment exceeding that which is available under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005, or under the Act s 32(3)(b) is necessary.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: For youthful offenders, rehabilitation is usually far more important than general deterrence. But this is only a general principle and does not apply automatically.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: For example, in cases of murder ‘there is much less room for the offender’s youth to have a significant role…’; it cannot overshadow the seriousness of that crime and the need to emphasise the importance of deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: It is unclear whether general deterrence principles apply where an offender is sentenced for charges which might have been dealt with in the Children’s Court but were in fact dealt with in a superior court.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: General deterrence is significant regardless of provocation or motive.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: In cases where a youthful offender carries out, or plans to carry out, acts of extreme violence, protection of our society and upholding fundamental values require that youth is diminished quite substantially in determining the weight to be given to general deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: General deterrence has minimal relevance when sentencing a child.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: The weight to be given to general deterrence in such cases will depend on multiple factors, including the seriousness of the offence and of the offending; the extent of the offender’s remorse (if any); and the offender’s rehabilitation prospects.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: Where general deterrence is a significant purpose, there is less scope for leniency based on the offender’s youth.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: This assumes the community will be aware of the sentence imposed for a given crime and gain awareness of the type of sentences imposed generally for that kind of conduct.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: Thus, there is a further assumption that an offender was aware, at the time of their offending, of the law and the consequences for its breach.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: The validity of these assumptions has been questioned by empirical research.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: However, the NSWCCA has noted that general deterrence ‘has another dimension – to maintain public confidence in the administration of justice’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: The level of community awareness of sentences being consistently imposed determines the extent to which they have a deterrent effect on others.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: In short, the deterrent effect of a sentence depends on the extent to which it is punitive (and will be so perceived by the community) and is communicated to those it is meant to deter.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: General deterrence, as a sentencing purpose, subjects an offender to a punishment that is more severe than would otherwise be the case.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: Additionally, the vulnerability and dependency often found in a domestic setting mean that violations are more serious and the need for deterrence is greater.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: It is also important to deter people taking the law into their own hands because ‘vigilante justice’ is a direct threat to the rule and authority of law.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

title: Specific deterrence: offending on orders, remorse and restitution
statement: Offending while subject to another court order (bail, parole, an intervention order) requires specific deterrence to be emphasised. Good rehabilitation prospects do not make specific deterrence irrelevant. Without genuine remorse, specific deterrence is particularly important; an offer of restitution may indicate remorse but is of limited consequence if not spontaneous or made only after discovery. Being on summons for another offence that did not lead to conviction is not relevant to specific deterrence.

refs.q: Relatedly, a person’s willingness to offend while subject to another court order, such as bail, parole, or an intervention order requires specific deterrence to be emphasised.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: But an offender’s efforts at rehabilitation and a finding they have good prospects of rehabilitation ‘does not render specific deterrence irrelevant’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: Where an offender does not exhibit genuine remorse, they have not shown an appreciation for their wrongdoing or good prospects of reform, and specific deterrence will be particularly important.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: In this regard, an offer of restitution may be an indicator of remorse, but if it is not spontaneous or if it is only made after discovery of the crime, it will be of limited consequence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: The fact that the offender was on summons for another offence, which did not lead to conviction, at the time of offending is not relevant to assessing the need for specific deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.2 – Specific deterrence

title: Rehabilitation: remorse and reform, indicators, and its place in the sentence
statement: Steps towards rehabilitation should be given due weight. Rehabilitation has two parts — remorse and reform — both of which must be demonstrated; less weight is given where genuine remorse is lacking or there is merely no further offending (but see TC, fn 751). Remorse is shown by post-offence conduct; it is error to reject it merely because it is inconsistent with a lack of remorse at the time of offending. A guilty plea may indicate remorse, but a not guilty plea is not itself a basis for finding no prospects; a spurious defence may reflect poorly. An absence of motive can make prospects hard to assess. Delay not attributable to the offender increases the emphasis on rehabilitation, so that rehabilitation under way is not halted. Rehabilitation is usually far more important than general deterrence for young offenders, but not automatically. Mental impairment does not mean an offender is incapable of rehabilitation. A short custodial term may reflect a rehabilitative aspect; a youthful first offender should if possible be given the opportunity to reform rather than custody. Only regret for the harm caused — not sorrow at being caught and punished — is remorse for sentencing purposes.

refs.q: The public interest is served by rehabilitating offenders to stop committing crimes, and a court should reward steps taken towards rehabilitation by giving them due weight in determining the sentence to be imposed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: Rehabilitation of the offender has two parts: remorse and reform. Both must be demonstrated, and less weight is given to rehabilitation if there is a lack of genuine remorse or a mere absence of further offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: Remorse is measured by post-conduct action and while a court is not bound to accept it, it is error not to do so because it was inconsistent with a lack of remorse at the time of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: A guilty plea may indicate remorse and rehabilitation, but a failure to plead guilty is not itself a basis for finding that an offender has no prospects of rehabilitation. Further, while entitled to run a defence, running a spurious and unmeritorious one may reflect poorly on an offender’s prospects for rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: The absence of a motive for the criminal conduct is also relevant as it can be difficult to assess an offender’s prospects of rehabilitation if a court cannot conclude whether the likelihood of reoffending has been reduced by the removal of the motive or reason for the crime.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: There is an increased emphasis on rehabilitation following a delay between the offending and the time of sentence that is not attributable to the offender. This is because rehabilitation that is underway should not be halted or endangered by the sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: Secondly, the courts have always emphasised the significance of rehabilitation when sentencing young offenders, it is ‘usually far more important than general deterrence’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: Similarly, an offender’s mental impairment may increase the need for community protection but does not mean a court should conclude that every mentally impaired offender is incapable of rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: While the circumstances of an offender often make rehabilitation a more important consideration than the other purposes, this is not an automatic process.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: Although a custodial sentence is not ordinarily considered rehabilitative, the shortness of the term may reflect a rehabilitative aspect.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: A youthful first offender should not, if it can be avoided, be given a custodial sentence. Instead, they should be given the opportunity to reform.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: There is a distinction between an offender’s sorrow at being caught and punished and regret for the harm caused by their actions – only that regret is remorse for sentencing purposes.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: But see TC v The Queen [2011] VSCA 190, [55].
This may be so even where the offender has committed very serious offences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: The reason for this emphasis is because society benefits by the successful rehabilitation of a young person who is led away from a life of crime.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: The type of sentence imposed will depend in part on whether rehabilitation is the sole, the dominant, or a minor purpose.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: A custodial sentence is ‘skewed towards retribution and deterrence’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has noted that the restrictions of imprisonment mean there is little opportunity or incentive for rehabilitation and the serious detriments imposed on the prisoner by custody impacts the community by creating individuals who are ill-equipped to function outside a penal environment and catalyses their renewed criminal activity on release.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: To assist certain offenders with treatment, a court may impose a Residential Treatment Order requiring them to reside in a specified facility for that purpose for up to five years.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

title: Protection of the community: indicators, s 6D, and dangerousness assessed at sentence
statement: Prior convictions showing a continuing disobedience of the law, reluctance to engage in treatment, or an incurable disorder that fuelled the offending may increase the importance of community protection. Under s 6D, when imprisonment is justified for a serious offender’s relevant offence, protection of the community becomes the principal purpose; because protection is always relevant, this has little impact except where mitigating factors call for a shorter term. The serious-danger assessment for an indefinite sentence is made at the time of sentencing, not as a prediction of dangerousness at the end of the sentence; on an application for review of the indefinite term (ss 18H, 18M) it is made as at the time of review. Invoking s 6D may produce a crushing sentence, which may have to be accepted if necessary to protect the community (as may an elderly offender’s likely death in jail).

refs.q: So too might their reluctance to participate in treatment for a disorder, or where they have a disorder that cannot presently be cured, and which fueled their offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: Firstly, section 6D of the Act provides that in sentencing a serious offender for a relevant offence, if the court considers that imprisonment is justified it must then regard protection of the community from the offender as the principal purpose for which the sentence is to be imposed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has noted that since community protection is always relevant, this direction has little impact except where mitigating factors might call for a shorter term.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: The assessment of serious dangerousness to the community is made at the time of sentencing. It is not a prediction of the offender’s future dangerousness when they complete their sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: Similarly, upon an application for review of the indefinite term, ss 18H and 18M of the Act require an assessment as at the time of review, as though the offender might then be released from custody.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: Invoking s 6D may also produce a crushing sentence, but if that is necessary to protect the community then it is a consequence that may have to be accepted, as might the fact that an elderly offender will likely die in jail.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: To achieve that purpose, the court may impose a longer sentence than is proportionate to the gravity of the offence given the objective circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

title: Comparing sentence types: the “loose hierarchy” of s 5(4)–(7) and the ordering the hard checks use
statement: Sections 5(4)–(7) create a loose hierarchy of sentencing options (3.2): imprisonment may not be imposed where a drug treatment order or a conditional CCO will serve the purposes; a drug treatment order cannot be imposed where a CCO will suffice; a CCO must not be imposed where a fine will do; and a fine cannot be imposed if a dismissal, discharge or adjournment is sufficient. The hierarchy does not mean there is a single less severe sentence that must be imposed. (app policy) Where a hard check must compare two sentence types (the s 6AAA notional sentence; a sentence indication), it uses this order: imprisonment (including a combination sentence) > CCO > fine > adjourned undertaking, discharge or dismissal (these three are not ranked among themselves). A comparison involving any other order (a DATO — the Manual does not say whether it is the “drug treatment order” of 3.2 — youth detention, CSTO, RTO, MTMO, indefinite sentence), or between the last three, is not settled by the Manual → caution, never error.

refs.q: The principle is also enshrined in s 5(3) of the Act and is expanded upon by ss 5(4)–(7) which ‘constrain[] the discretion of sentencing courts to impose particular sanctions where another sanction would be of sufficient severity, th[us] creat[ing] a loose hierarchy of sentencing options’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.2 – Parsimony

refs.q: A sentence of imprisonment also may not be imposed where a drug treatment order or conditional Community Corrections Order (‘CCO’) will serve the sentencing purposes. Further, a drug treatment order cannot be imposed where a CCO will suffice, a CCO must not be imposed where a fine will do, and a fine cannot be imposed if a dismissal, discharge or adjournment is sufficient.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.2 – Parsimony

refs.q: This hierarchy does not mean there is a single less severe sentence that must be imposed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.2 – Parsimony
